title: Chocolate Phuljhadi: The No-Bake Sparkler Sweet Children Can Make for Diwali
excerpt: Biscuit sticks dipped in melted chocolate and rolled in sprinkles until they look like little sparklers — no baking, ready as soon as the chocolate sets. Slurrp's version makes 12 sticks; a viral biscuit-dough version with edible silver dust is dividing the internet this Diwali.
body:
• Chocolate phuljhadi are biscuit sticks dipped in melted chocolate and rolled in sprinkles to look like sparklers — no baking, and ready as soon as the chocolate sets.
  • You need five things: 12 long biscuit or pretzel sticks, 1 cup of chopped chocolate, 1 teaspoon of coconut oil or butter, a quarter cup of sprinkles, and 15-20 minutes of fridge time.
  • It is a make-with-children recipe: the only heat is melting chocolate over simmering water, and children can do the dipping and rolling themselves.
  • A second, viral version shapes crushed biscuit dough around skewers and finishes it with edible silver lustre dust — prettier, fussier, and currently dividing the internet.

Chocolate phuljhadi is a fun one to put together, especially if there are kids around. Biscuit sticks are dipped in melted chocolate and rolled in sprinkles until they look like little sparklers. Nothing needs baking, and it is ready as soon as the chocolate sets, writes Simran Makkar in Slurrp's recipe.

How to Make Them

Melt 1 cup of chopped dark or milk chocolate with 1 teaspoon of coconut oil or butter in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water, stirring until smooth and glossy. Let it cool for a couple of minutes so it is not too runny — chocolate that is too hot slides straight off the stick.

Dip each of the 12 pretzel sticks or long biscuit sticks (Pocky or breadsticks both work) into the chocolate, covering about two-thirds of its length, and tap gently against the edge of the bowl to let the extra drip off. Roll the coated part in the sprinkles — a quarter cup of colourful sprinkles is the classic finish, with crushed nuts or desiccated coconut as alternatives — while the chocolate is still wet. Place the sticks on a lined tray and refrigerate for 15 to 20 minutes, until the chocolate sets firm.

"Nothing needs baking, and it is ready as soon as the chocolate sets, writes Simran Makkar in Slurrp's recipe ."

The Viral Version Dividing the Internet

A second phuljhadi is having a moment online. In the viral video covered by Indulge Express, the maker crushes 10-12 chocolate chip biscuits with 1.5 to 2 tablespoons of condensed milk into a dough, rolls it around skewers, freezes it for 15 minutes, dips it in 80 grams of melted dark chocolate, coats it in crushed rock sugar and finishes with edible silver lustre dust for a metallic, sparkler-real finish. It looks more like the real thing — and takes three times as long, which is roughly the split in the comments.

Serving Notes for Diaspora Kitchens

Every ingredient is a standard supermarket item in the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf: Pocky and pretzel sticks stand in for Indian biscuit sticks, and any melting chocolate works. Make them the morning of a Diwali party and keep them refrigerated until serving; the sticks soften if they sit in a warm room for hours. Stand them upright in a glass, sparkler-ends up, and they double as the table decoration.

One safety note that matters in a festival built around real sparklers: label the plate. These look enough like the real thing that a small child should not be left to guess which ones are edible — keep the edible version on the dessert table and the lit version outside, as separate rituals.
